'''''Barbarea vulgaris''''', called '''wintercress''' (usual common name), or alternatively '''winter rocket''', '''rocketcress''', '''yellow rocketcress''', '''yellow rocket''', '''wound rocket''', '''herb barbara''', '''creases''', or '''creasy greens''', is a [[Biennial plant|biennial]] herb of the genus ''[[Barbarea]]'', belonging to the family [[Brassicaceae]].

==Description==
The plant grows to {{cvt|80|cm}} high and {{cvt|25|cm|frac=2}} wide.<ref name="tfb">{{Cite book |last=Francis-Baker |first=Tiffany |title=Concise Foraging Guide |date=2021 |publisher=[[Bloomsbury Publishing|Bloomsbury]] |isbn=978-1-4729-8474-6 |series=[[The Wildlife Trusts]] |location=London |page=62 }}</ref> The stem is ribbed and hairless, branched at the base. It has basal [[Rosette (botany)|rosette]]s of shiny, dark green leaves. The basal leaves are stalked and lyre-pinnatifid, that is with a large terminal lobe and smaller lower lobes. The cauline leaves are smaller, ovate, toothed, or lobed. The flowers are borne in spring in dense terminal clusters above the [[Leaf|foliage]]. They are {{cvt|7|-|9|mm|frac=8}} long, with four bright yellow petals. The flowering period extends from about April through July. The fruits are a [[silique]]s (seed capsules) of length {{cvt|15|-|30|mm|frac=8}}.<ref name="SIG:2023">{{cite web |title=Barbarea W. T. Aiton spp. |url=https://seedidguide.idseed.org/fact_sheets/barbarea-spp-4/ |website=seedidguide.idseed.org |publisher=International Seed Morphology Association |access-date=19 July 2026 |date=27 March 2023 |ISBN=978-1-7753419-0-1 |archive-date=21 April 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250421082950/https://seedidguide.idseed.org/fact_sheets/barbarea-spp-4/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

A single ''B. vulgaris'' plant can produce up to 88,000 seeds per year, its seeds are long lived, remaining viable for 10–20 years. Wintercress is also known to reproduce [[Vegetative reproduction|vegetatively]] from roots or buds near its base, presenting as ''cauline rosettes''.<ref name="SIG:2023" /><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Aarssen |first1=Lonnie W. |title=THE BIOLOGY OF CANADIAN WEEDS: 50. Hypochoeris radicata L. |journal=Canadian Journal of Plant Science |date=April 1981 |volume=61 |issue=2 |page=374 |doi=10.4141/cjps81-051 |url=https://cdnsciencepub.com/doi/epdf/10.4141/cjps81-051 |access-date=2 July 2026 |publisher=Canadian Science Publishing |location=Ottawa, Ontario, Canada }}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
Formally, ''B. vulgaris'' was first published and described by [[William Aiton]] in his ''[[Hortus Kewensis]]'' (1812).<ref>Vol.4 on page 109.</ref> Some references still mention [[Robert Brown (botanist, born 1773)|Robert Brown]]<ref>{{cite web |title=''Barbarea vulgaris'' R.Br. is an accepted name |url=http://www.theplantlist.org/tpl1.1/record/kew-2669712 |publisher=theplantlist.org |access-date=13 November 2017 |archive-date=27 November 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181127022451/http://www.theplantlist.org/tpl1.1/record/kew-2669712 |url-status=live }}</ref> as the author. Indeed, botanists believe that Brown was the actual author of the first botanical description of ''B. vulgaris'' in the description of the family [[Brassicaceae]].<ref>{{cite book |title=Brassicaceae ''Barbarea vulgaris'' W.T.Aiton |volume=4 |url=http://www.ipni.org/ipni/idPlantNameSearch.do?id=29455-2 |access-date=13 November 2017 }}</ref><ref>Hortus Kew. ed. 2.</ref> However, W. T. Aiton, the publishing author, did not mention or indicate Brown's name for Brassicaceae; therefore, W. T. Aiton is author of the Brassicaceae novelties in this work.<ref>{{cite book |title=Brassicaceae ''Barbarea vulgaris'' W.T.Aiton |volume=4 |url=http://www.ipni.org/ipni/idPlantNameSearch.do?id=29455-2 |access-date=13 November 2017 |archive-date=14 November 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171114040931/http://www.ipni.org/ipni/idPlantNameSearch.do?id=29455-2 |url-status=live }}</ref>

''B. vulgaris'' has various common names of which the most commonly used is 'wintercress',<ref>Gleason, H.A. Illustrated Flora of the NE United States and Adjacent Canada, 1952.</ref> which can also be used for the entire genus ''[[Barbarea]]''. Many other common names are listed in various sources, including (in alphabetical order), 'creases', 'creasy greens', 'cressy-greens', 'English wintercress', 'herb-Barbaras', 'rocket cress', and 'yellow rocket'.<ref name="Grin">{{cite web |title=Taxon: ''Barbarea vulgaris'' W. T. Aiton |url=https://npgsweb.ars-grin.gov/gringlobal/taxonomydetail.aspx?id=6491 |publisher=ars-grin.gov |access-date=15 November 2017 }}</ref><ref name="south-carolina">{{Cite book |last1=McMillan |first1=Patrick D. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LYxyEAAAQBAJ |title=A Guide to the Wildflowers of South Carolina |last2=Jr |first2=Richard Dwight Porcher |last3=Rayner |first3=Douglas A. |last4=White |first4=David B. |date=15 August 2022 |publisher=Univ of South Carolina Press |isbn=978-1-64336-264-9 |language=en |page=527 }}</ref><ref name="eastern-cherokee">{{Cite journal |last=WHITE |first=MAX E. |date=1975 |title=Contemporary Usage of Native Plant Foods by the Eastern Cherokees |journal=Appalachian Journal |volume=2 |issue=4 |pages=323–326 |jstor=40932067 |issn=0090-3779 }}</ref> Two additional names sometimes used, 'bittercress' and 'upland cress' are ambiguous; the name 'bittercress' usually signifies various species of the genus ''[[Cardamine]]'', and 'upland cress' usually signifies ''[[Barbarea verna|B. verna]]''.

===Etymology===
The genus name ''Barbarea'' derives from [[Saint Barbara]], the patron saint of [[artillerymen]] and miners, as this plant in the past was used to soothe the wounds caused by explosions.<ref name=Readers>{{cite book |year=1981 |title=Reader's Digest Field Guide to the Wild Flowers of Britain |page=46 |publisher=[[Reader's Digest]] |isbn=978-0-276-00217-5 }}</ref> The species Latin name ''vulgaris'' means "common".<ref>Allen J. Coombes {{google books|capqDQYT_VYC&|The A to Z of Plant Names: A Quick Reference Guide to 4000 Garden Plants|page=65 }}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
Native to Eurasia and North Africa, it is [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] in many parts of North America and New Zealand as a weed.<ref name="Grin" />

===Range===
It is found in [[temperate]] North Africa within Algeria and Tunisia. Also in Asia, within Afghanistan, Armenia, Azerbaijan, the [[Caucasus]], China (in the provinces of [[Heilongjiang]], [[Jiangsu]], [[Jilin]] and [[Xinjiang]]), Georgia, Iran, Iraq, Japan (in the provinces [[Hokkaido]], [[Honshu]], [[Kyushu]], [[Ryukyu Islands]] and [[Shikoku]]), Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Mongolia, [[Siberia]], Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Turkey. It is also found in tropical parts of Asia, such as India, Pakistan and Sri Lanka.

In eastern Europe, it is found within Belarus, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Moldova and Ukraine. In middle Europe, it is in Austria, Belgium, the Czech Republic, Germany, Hungary, the Netherlands, Poland, Slovakia and Switzerland. In northern Europe, in Denmark, Ireland, Sweden and United Kingdom. In southeastern Europe, within Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Croatia, Greece, Italy, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Romania, Serbia and Slovenia. Lastly, it is found in southwestern Europe, it is found in France, Portugal and Spain.<ref name="Grin"/>

=== Habitat ===
The plant prefers fresh or moist places, on roadsides, along rivers, in arable land, wastelands and docklands, or on the slopes and in ditches, at an altitude of {{cvt|0|-|2500|m}} above sea level.<ref name="iucn status 12 November 2021" /> In Britain, it can be found in hedgerows and the edges of woodlands.<ref name="tfb" />

It also prefers to grow in siliceous, calcareous, sandy, alluvial and clay soils.<ref name="iucn status 12 November 2021" />

==Ecology==

=== Natural chemotypes with distinct ecology ===
A pubescent type (the "P-type") has been described from southern Scandinavia and Russia. While this chemotype is rare in Scandinavia, it seems to be dominant in Russia according to the only survey made so far.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Christensen |first1=Stina |last2=Heimes |first2=Christine |last3=Agerbirk |first3=Niels |last4=Kuzina |first4=Vera |last5=Olsen |first5=Carl Erik |last6=Hauser |first6=Thure Pavlo |date=1 May 2014 |title=Different Geographical Distributions of Two Chemotypes of ''Barbarea vulgaris'' that Differ in Resistance to Insects and a Pathogen |journal=Journal of Chemical Ecology |language=en |volume=40 |issue=5 |pages=491–501 |doi=10.1007/s10886-014-0430-4 |pmid=24777484 |bibcode=2014JCEco..40..491C |s2cid=9809723 |issn=1573-1561 }}</ref> This type has atypical chemistry and is devoid of resistance to the diamondback moth and the flea beetle ''[[Phyllotreta nemorum]]''. The P-type belongs morphologically to the variety ''B. vulgaris'' var. ''arcuata'', but may also be identical to the variety originally described as ''Barbarea'' ''arcuata'' Rchb. var. ''pubescens'' N. Busch. In this context, the usual type of ''B. vulgaris'' var. ''arcuata'' is called the "G-type" (for glabrous (hairless) leaves). This type is reported to be dominant in Central Europe.<ref name=":0" /> On a genomic scale, more than 22.000 genes (89% of those tested) were found to have fixed differences between the two types.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Byrne |first1=Stephen L. |last2=Erthmann |first2=Pernille Østerbye |last3=Agerbirk |first3=Niels |last4=Bak |first4=Søren |last5=Hauser |first5=Thure Pavlo |last6=Nagy |first6=Istvan |last7=Paina |first7=Cristiana |last8=Asp |first8=Torben |date=17 January 2017 |title=The genome sequence of ''Barbarea vulgaris'' facilitates the study of ecological biochemistry |journal=Scientific Reports |language=en |volume=7 |issue=1 |article-number=40728 |doi=10.1038/srep40728 |pmid=28094805 |pmc=5240624 |issn=2045-2322 |bibcode=2017NatSR...740728B |doi-access=free }}</ref>

A chemotype with deviating [[glucosinolate]] content has been described from Western and Central Europe and named the "NAS-type" (because it is dominated by the glucosinolate glucoNASturtiin. This type has increased resistance to some specialized insects. In this context, the usual chemotype of ''B. vulgaris'' is called the "BAR" type (because it is dominated by glucoBARbarin).<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=van Leur |first1=Hanneke |last2=Raaijmakers |first2=Ciska E. |last3=van Dam |first3=Nicole M. |date=2006 |title=A heritable glucosinolate polymorphism within natural populations of ''Barbarea vulgaris'' |journal=Phytochemistry |volume=67 |issue=12 |pages=1214–1223 |doi=10.1016/j.phytochem.2006.04.021 |issn=0031-9422 |pmid=16777152 |bibcode=2006PChem..67.1214V }}</ref>

While the P-type and G-type differ in multiple genetic, chemical and morphological features, the NAS and BAR types seem to be a simple [[monogenic]] variation.<ref name=":1" /> For this reason, it has been suggested to refer to NAS and BAR forms (from the lowest botanical rank forma) and P- and G-types. Indeed, occasional NAS form plants in Central Europe were found to be G-type by a set of genetic markers.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Agerbirk |first1=Niels |last2=Olsen |first2=Carl Erik |last3=Heimes |first3=Christine |last4=Christensen |first4=Stina |last5=Bak |first5=Søren |last6=Hauser |first6=Thure P. |date=2015 |title=Multiple hydroxyphenethyl glucosinolate isomers and their tandem mass spectrometric distinction in a geographically structured polymorphism in the crucifer ''Barbarea vulgaris'' |journal=Phytochemistry |language=en |volume=115 |pages=130–142 |doi=10.1016/j.phytochem.2014.09.003 |pmid=25277803 |bibcode=2015PChem.115..130A }}</ref>

=== Natural insect resistance ===
Most ''B. vulgaris'' genotypes are naturally resistant to some insect species that are otherwise specialized on the crucifer family. In the case of diamondback moth (''[[Plutella xylostella]]'') and the flea beetle ''[[Phyllotreta nemorum]]'', the resistance is caused by [[saponin]]s.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3" /><ref name=":4" /><ref name=":5" /> Glucosinolates such as [[glucobarbarin]] and [[glucobrassicin]] are used as a cue for egg-laying by female cabbage white butterflies such as ''[[Pieris rapae]]''. Indeed, the larvae of this butterfly thrive well on this plant. Diamondback moth females are also stimulated by these chemicals, but the larvae die due to the content of saponins which are apparently not sensed by the moths. This phenomenon has been tested for biological insect control: ''B. vulgaris'' plants are placed in a field and attract much of the diamondback moth egg load. As the larvae die shortly after hatching, this kind of insect control has been named "[[dead-end trap cropping]]".<ref>Shelton, A. M. and B. A. Nault (2004) "Dead-end trap cropping: a technique to improve management of the diamondback moth," ''Crop Protection'' '''23''': 497-503.</ref><!-- BiolConserv137:248. -->

===Ecological impact ===
''B. vulgaris'' is listed as a ''Class 3: Secondary Noxious Weed'' by the [[Canadian Food Inspection Agency]] due to difficulties preventing its small seed, {{cvt|1.2|-|1.5|mm}} long by {{cvt|1.0|-|1.2|mm}} wide, from contaminating seed stocks of other small-seeded crops, e.g. grain, hay and vegetables.<ref name="SIG:2023" />

== Uses ==
The young leaves can be eaten raw or cooked.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Niering |first1=William A. |author-link1=William Niering |last2=Olmstead |first2=Nancy C. |title=The Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Wildflowers, Eastern Region |year=1985 |orig-date=1979 |publisher=Knopf |isbn=0-394-50432-1 |page=425 }}</ref> The buds and flowers are also edible,<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Elias |first1=Thomas S. |title=Edible Wild Plants: A North American Field Guide to Over 200 Natural Foods |last2=Dykeman |first2=Peter A. |publisher=[[Sterling Publishing|Sterling]] |year=2009 |isbn=978-1-4027-6715-9 |location=New York |page=99 |oclc=244766414 |orig-date=1982 }}</ref> as are the flower shoots after cooking.<ref name="tfb" /> It can also be used as a dead-end [[trap crop]] for [[diamondback moth]], the caterpillar of which is a pest on cruciferous plants like [[cabbage]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Badenes-Perez |first1=Francisco R. |last2=Reichelt |first2=Michael |last3=Gershenzon |first3=Jonathan |last4=Heckel |first4=David G. |date=February 2014 |title=Using plant chemistry and insect preference to study the potential of Barbarea (Brassicaceae) as a dead-end trap crop for diamondback moth (Lepidoptera: Plutellidae) |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0031942213004445 |journal=Phytochemistry |language=en |volume=98 |pages=137–144 |doi=10.1016/j.phytochem.2013.11.009 |pmid=24342111 |bibcode=2014PChem..98..137B |url-access=subscription |archive-date=24 February 2021 |access-date=7 June 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210224181515/https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0031942213004445 |url-status=live }}</ref>
